name: ott
desc: Tool for writing definitions of programming languages and calculi
why: A tool for writing formal semantics of programming languages and calculi, a genuine door into programming language theory.

brief.what_it_is: Ott is a command-line tool for writing definitions of programming languages and calculi. You write a language's syntax and semantics in a concise ASCII notation that looks like informal mathematics. From that one source file it can generate a LaTeX file for typeset output, plus Coq, HOL, Isabelle/HOL and Lem versions of the definition, and an OCaml syntax module. It can also run as a filter over LaTeX or proof-assistant files, parsing embedded terms and replacing them with typeset versions. Parsing the input also sort-checks it, so simple errors such as inconsistent judgement forms or metavariable naming are caught early.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to ease the move from informal to formal mathematics: write the definition once in a clear, editable ASCII notation without LaTeX noise, typeset it for papers, and generate formal definitions for proof assistants from the same source.
brief.how_it_works: Ott reads a grammar-and-rules source file in its ASCII notation and parses and sort-checks it. Annotations in the source control what gets generated. It then emits the chosen backend output, such as LaTeX, Coq, HOL, Isabelle or Lem. It can also generate helper functions automatically, including free variables, single and multiple substitutions, subgrammar checks and binding auxiliaries. The README says only a fully concrete representation of binding, without quotienting by alpha-equivalence, is fully supported.

commands_seen.context: Runs Ott on the bundled test file tests/test10.ott and writes LaTeX to test10.tex and Coq to test10.v. The README says Isabelle, HOL and Lem outputs use -o test10.thy, -o test10Script.sml and -o test10.lem.
Installs the latest released Ott from the opam package repository. The README says the Emacs mode and documentation then land under the opam prefix.
Adds the Coq released opam repository. Needed before installing the Coq auxiliary files.
Installs the Ott auxiliary files for Coq, if you want to use Ott output with the Coq proof assistant.
Run inside a GitHub checkout to install Ott from local source.
Rebuilds and reinstalls after local changes to a checkout. Short form is opam upgrade -w ott.
Builds the ott binary in the bin/ subdirectory when building without opam. The README also lists make world as equivalent.
Builds with ocamlc instead of ocamlopt. The README says this may run Ott significantly slower.
Run in the coq/ subdirectory after make, to install the Coq auxiliary files into Coq's user-contrib.

brief.install_notes: Easiest route is opam 2.0 or later (the README says opam 1 versions are no longer supported): opam install ott. Optional Coq support needs the coq-released opam repository added first, then opam install coq-ott. Building from source needs OCaml 4.07.0 or later plus the ocamlgraph package; the README says it builds with OCaml 4.07.0 and 4.14.0 and ocamlgraph 1.8.8. Without opam, run make in the checkout, and run make inside coq/ then make install for the Coq files. An Emacs mode (emacs/ott-mode.el) and a VS Code extension are also available.
brief.standout: It is a single ASCII source that feeds both a typeset paper appendix and formal proof-assistant definitions, and it checks the sorts and judgement forms as it parses. The filter mode, which typesets Ott terms embedded in existing LaTeX or proof files, is a practical touch. The README lists real systems built with it, including TAPL-style calculi, POPLmark Fsub, the Leroy JFP96 ML module system, Lightweight Java and an OCaml-light semantics.
brief.status: Maintained, though thinly. The README says As of 2024, Ott remains in continuous use, and the GitHub repo shows a Docker CI badge on master. The README also says the issue tracker is now GitHub's, though resources for fixing issues are very limited. I did not find a release date or last-commit date in what I fetched.
brief.caveats: The README warns that resources for fixing issues are very limited. Only the fully concrete binding representation is fully supported; the locally-nameless backend is experimental, and the menhir parser and pretty printer are marked experimental. Some POPLmark examples would need explicit alpha-conversion to capture the intended semantics, per the README footnote. Building from source needs a fairly specific OCaml setup. The Coq and HOL outputs are generated definitions, so proof scripts are separate. The licence is BSD-style, per the README. I did not check platform support beyond the opam route.
quotes: Ott is a tool for writing definitions of programming languages and calculi.
Most simply, Ott can be used to aid informal LaTeX mathematics.
As of 2024, Ott remains in continuous use.
Please now use the github issue tracker (though our resources for fixing issues are very limited)
